metaDescription: Six restaurant-style deep fryers compared by gas or electric power, oil capacity, BTU or watt rating, tube design and the ventilation and safety each needs.
expertTake: The MoTak 40 lb tube-style gas fryer is the pick for a small kitchen that wants a floor-standing workhorse on casters, and the CookRite ATFS-40 is the traditional three-tube alternative with standby pilots. The 25.4 quart dual tank electric is the pick where gas is not available. Anyone buying one for a home garage needs to plan the fuel supply, ventilation and fire safety first.
introParagraphs: A restaurant fryer is built for volume. Where a countertop home fryer holds a few quarts and shuts off, a floor-standing gas fryer holds around 40 pounds of oil, heats with a bank of burners and recovers temperature fast enough to cook basket after basket through a dinner rush.

That capability brings obligations that a home appliance never does: a gas supply or a heavy electrical circuit, ventilation, a safe place for hot oil, fire protection and, for a business, local code approval. This guide ranks the lineup by output, build and how much planning each demands, and it treats the plan as part of the purchase.

products.name: MoTak MGF3-N-C 40 lb Natural Gas Tube Fryer, 90,000 BTU
products.description:
MoTak's fryer delivers 90,000 BTU on natural gas, holds 40 pounds of oil and uses a tube-style fry pot, a design where burner tubes run through the oil, with a 200 to 400 degree thermostat and mobile casters. The body is stainless steel and about 15.5 inches wide.

Tube design is the classic restaurant layout. Heat transfers from the tubes into the oil directly, which gives quick recovery, and the space below the tubes forms a cool zone where crumbs settle instead of burning. That makes it well suited to breaded foods such as fried chicken, onion rings and tempura, as the listing states. The casters let you move it for cleaning, though a gas line connection limits where it can go.

A gas fryer demands installation by a qualified person, a proper vent hood and a regulated gas supply, and it should never run unattended. Keep the oil at the right level, filter it daily in service and replace it on a schedule. Follow local fire and building codes, and keep a suitable fire extinguisher and suppression system in place.
products.bestFor: Small restaurants and food trucks with gas service.
pros: Tube-style pot with a cool zone for crumbs
cons: Needs gas supply, venting and professional installation

products.name: CookRite ATFS-40 3-Tube Natural Gas Fryer, 102,000 BTU

specList.label: Burners
specList.value: Three heavy-duty tubes with standby pilots

products.description:
CookRite's ATFS-40 rates 102,000 BTU with three heavy-duty burner tubes and standby pilots, a cooling zone at the bottom of the tank and nickel-plated baskets with a wire mesh crumb screen. The structure is stainless steel and described as corrosion resistant.

Standby pilots are a feature of traditional restaurant fryers: a small flame stays lit so the main burners ignite quickly and the machine recovers fast when the thermostat calls. The cooling zone keeps food residue from touching the hot oil, which extends oil life. Against the MoTak, the CookRite has slightly higher BTU and a more conventional layout, but no stated casters or thermostat range in the excerpt reviewed.

Installation matters most. A gas fryer needs a qualified installer, a rated hood and a gas regulator, and it must sit on a level, non-combustible surface. Filter the oil daily, clean the crumb screen and inspect the pilots and burners for soot. Never leave a gas fryer unattended, and train staff on emergency shutoff. Because pilots burn all day, check them at opening and closing, and shut the gas valve at night. A gas smell is an emergency: leave the building, avoid switches and call the gas supplier or emergency services from a safe place.
products.bestFor: Kitchens that want a conventional three-tube gas fryer.
pros: Cooling zone protects oil from crumbs
cons: Needs gas, hood and professional installation
Thermostat range not stated in the listing text reviewed

products.name: VEVOR 40 lb Natural Gas Floor Fryer, 90,000 BTU Triple Burner
products.description:
VEVOR's floor-standing gas fryer pairs a 40 pound tank with triple burners rated 90,000 BTU, a mechanical thermostat dial from 200 to 400 degrees and a cool zone design. The listing says the cool zone avoids scrap carbonization and a bottom oil drain makes oil changes easier.

It competes directly with the MoTak, with the same BTU rating and oil capacity. The difference is a more value-oriented position and a stated mechanical thermostat, which is simple and easy to repair. A mechanical dial lacks the display of a digital control, but it is dependable in a hot kitchen. The cool zone is a standard restaurant feature that keeps crumbs from burning in the oil.

Plan the installation: gas line, regulator, hood, a level floor and clearance from combustibles. Filter the oil in service, drain it through the bottom valve with care and let it cool first. A tank of 40 pounds of hot oil is a serious hazard, so train everyone who uses it. Keep an appropriate extinguisher nearby. Check a mechanical dial against a probe thermometer now and then, since it drifts over time.
products.bestFor: Cost-conscious kitchens that need a 40 pound gas fryer.
pros: Mechanical thermostat is simple and repairable
cons: Short brand history in heavy service

products.name: VEVOR Dual Tank 3000W Electric Countertop Fryer, 2 x 8.5-Qt Oil
products.description:
VEVOR's electric countertop unit has two separate tanks, each holding up to 8.5 quarts of oil, with dual heating elements delivering 3000 watts and a temperature range of 122 to 392 degrees with a timer. The listing says water capacity is 11.6 quarts each, so oil fills lower than the tank volume.

Electric avoids the gas line, which makes it the route into commercial frying for a food stall or a kitchen without gas. Two tanks let you fry two foods at different temperatures, and the wide temperature range reaches down to a 122 degree warming level. The trade-off is power: 3000 watts is a heavy load, so it needs a dedicated circuit and cannot be plugged into an ordinary kitchen outlet.

Check the circuit and plug type before ordering, since a 3000 watt unit draws about 25 amps at 120 volts. Fill oil only to the oil line, let it cool before draining and filter each tank separately. Keep the unit on a stable, heat-resistant counter with ventilation above it. Because each tank is only 8.5 quarts of oil, recovery between baskets is slower than in a 40 pound gas fryer, so cook in modest loads and avoid frozen blocks that crash the temperature. Run the two tanks at different settings only when you need to, since a tank held at low heat for hours degrades its oil.
products.bestFor: Stalls and cafes without gas that need two tanks.
cons: Smaller volume than a 40 pound gas fryer

products.name: 3500W 25.4-Qt Dual Tank Countertop Electric Fryer

specList.label: Tanks
specList.value: Two, each with thermostat and on/off switch

products.description:
This dual-tank countertop fryer carries 1750 watts per side, 3500 watts in total, with 25.4 quarts of capacity across two separate frying tanks that each have their own thermostat and on and off switch. The construction is thickened stainless steel.

Independent controls are the key feature. Each tank runs at its own temperature and can be shut off when not needed, which saves power during slow service and lets you hold one tank at a lower temperature. The total capacity is larger than the 8.5 quart electric above, which suits a busier kitchen. It is a bigger, heavier machine with a larger power draw.

A 3500 watt draw is about 29 amps at 120 volts, so confirm the circuit and consider whether the unit needs 240 volts. Fill each tank to the line, filter oil daily and keep the thermostats calibrated. Use a hood or adequate ventilation, and never leave a heated tank unattended. The on and off switch for each side is also a quiet energy saver, since you can run one tank during slow hours and bring the second up only for the rush. Wipe the exterior daily and check the cord and plug for heat discoloration, which signals a loose connection or an overloaded circuit.
products.bestFor: Busy kitchens that want independent tanks and more capacity.
pros: Independent thermostat and switch per tank
cons: Very large and heavy for a counter
Brand is not identified in the title

products.name: VEVOR Outdoor Propane Fryer, Dual-Tank 16-Qt x2, 50,000 BTU Each
products.description:
VEVOR's outdoor model is a floor-standing propane fryer with two stainless tanks, 16 quarts each for 32 quarts or 8 gallons total, two cast burners of 50,000 BTU each and a hanging rod for draining or keeping food warm. The listing targets catering events and camps.

Propane makes it portable: no gas line or electrical circuit, just a tank, which suits outdoor events and mobile service. Two tanks with separate burners let you fry two foods at different temperatures, and the thermometer on each helps. It cooks at volume, and it is the only model here that must never be used indoors.

Outdoor propane frying is hazardous. Set the unit on level ground away from structures and overhangs, keep a safe distance from combustibles, use a regulator and hose rated for propane, check connections for leaks with soapy water and keep a suitable extinguisher at hand. Let the oil cool completely before moving it, and never fry in rain or wind. Keep children and pets well away from the area, use a pot-lowering technique that avoids splashing and never overfill a tank, because a boil-over onto an open flame is the most common cause of outdoor fryer fires. A fire extinguisher rated for grease and a clear exit path are essential at every event.
products.bestFor: Caterers and camps that fry outdoors without power.
pros: Two 16 quart tanks with separate burners

buyingCriteria.explanation: The MoTak, CookRite and VEVOR floor fryers run on natural gas, the VEVOR outdoor unit on propane and the two countertop models on electricity. Gas has the highest output, electric avoids gas lines but needs a heavy circuit and propane is for outdoor use. The fuel decides where the machine can go.

The CookRite lists 102,000 BTU, the MoTak and VEVOR floor models 90,000, the outdoor propane unit 50,000 per burner, and the electrics 3000 and 3500 watts. A BTU is a gas measure and a watt an electric one, and 3412 BTU per hour equals 1000 watts, so 3500 watts is about 12,000 BTU per hour, a small fraction of a gas floor fryer. Compare like with like. That conversion also explains why electric countertop units top out at modest output: a 3500 watt fryer supplies roughly one eighth of the heat of a 90,000 BTU gas floor fryer, so it recovers more slowly and fits lower-volume menus. For a busy dinner service the gas machines are in a different league, and electric units suit cafes, bars and food stalls.

The gas floor fryers hold 40 pounds of oil, the electric dual-tank 25.4 quarts or 2 x 8.5 quarts, the propane unit 32 quarts. Bigger oil volumes recover faster and handle more baskets. Match capacity to your peak hour.

Tube fryers like the MoTak and CookRite run burner tubes through the oil with a cool zone below, which keeps crumbs from burning and extends oil life. Open-pot fryers are easier to clean but burn crumbs. Breaded foods benefit from tubes.

Gas fryers need a qualified installer, a hood and a regulated supply, and a business must follow local fire and health codes. Electric units need a dedicated circuit. Budget for the installation, not just the machine.

Bottom drains, filtering routines and daily cleaning are part of commercial frying. A 40 pound tank of hot oil is a serious burn hazard. Train staff, use proper containers and keep fire protection in place.

maintenance.why: Crumbs burn and degrade oil quickly. Daily filtering extends oil life.
Carbon and polymerized oil build up on tank walls. A boil-out with a cleaner restores heat transfer.
Soot and a weak flame signal poor combustion.
A drifting thermostat overheats or undercooks. Verify with a thermometer.
Leaks are a fire and explosion hazard. Use soapy water or a professional check.

faq.q: Do I need a hood for a commercial fryer?
faq.a: Generally yes for gas and for any business use. Local codes usually require a hood and fire suppression above commercial frying equipment, and insurers often insist on it. Ask your local inspector and a qualified installer before you buy, since the hood can cost as much as the fryer.

faq.q: Can I run a commercial electric fryer on a home outlet?
faq.a: Usually not. A 3000 watt unit draws about 25 amps at 120 volts, which exceeds a standard 15 or 20 amp circuit. Have an electrician install a dedicated circuit with the right receptacle, and do not use an extension cord, which can overheat under that load.

faq.q: How often should I change the oil?
faq.a: When it darkens, foams, smokes at a lower temperature or smells off. Daily filtering extends its life, and many kitchens keep a simple log of changes. Fish and heavily breaded foods shorten oil life, so change it sooner on a menu heavy in those.
Only outdoors, on level ground away from structures, with a rated regulator and hose and leak checks.
A fryer with burner tubes running through the oil and a cool zone below, which extends oil life.

A business usually needs permits and inspections for gas, electrical work and fire safety, and a health permit for food service. Check local rules before ordering, because a fryer that fails inspection cannot be used no matter what it cost.
